meaning: The external form of the problem of evil needs the premise that there is evil, asserted as true (ST I q.2 a.3 obj. 1). O'Connor's emotivism (moral statements have no truth value), his own gloss (what has no truth value is not true) and his classification of badness ascriptions as moral and the bridge that the evil premise says something is bad (q.2 a.3 obj. 1) jointly contradict that premise. Each bridge is its own sourced statement. The theorem uses only the premise's truth, so it also covers the stronger 'objectively true'. It does not touch the internal form, which O'Connor can run on the theist's own standard (see POE-CATHOLIC-CONSISTENT-WITH-EVIL). Proof shape, stated plainly: the derivation is three steps (the evil premise is moral because it says something is bad; emotivism then denies it a truth value; the gloss then denies it truth, against the external premise). No premise already states the conclusion. The philosophical content is in the four separately sourced premises: emotivism as a universal over moral sentences, the gloss fixing that lacking truth value excludes truth, the classification of badness ascriptions as moral, and the reading of the evil premise as saying something is bad.
